title: Why Should Christians Give Their Money Away?
subtitle: Giving is not a tax the church levies on the faithful. It is the medicine that breaks greed's grip and the practice that moves treasure where moth and rust cannot reach. A Christian reckoning with the tithe, the open hand, and the joy of letting go.

parts.title: The Hand That Will Not Open
parts.body:
You meant to give. You really did. You saw the need, felt the tug, opened the app, and then some quiet calculation started in the back of your mind, the same one that always starts, and by the time it finished you had given less than you meant to, or given nothing, or told yourself you would give next month when things were more settled. They are never more settled. The calculation always wins, and you walk away with a faint unease you have learned not to look at too closely, the sense that your hand closes more easily than it opens.

Maybe your struggle is fear. The math is genuinely tight, the future genuinely uncertain, and every dollar that leaves feels like a dollar removed from the thin wall between your family and disaster. You are not greedy, you tell yourself, you are just being responsible, and there is truth in that, and also the responsible voice and the fearful voice sound exactly alike, and you can no longer tell which one is speaking.

Maybe your struggle is that you give, even give a lot, and it has gone cold. You write the check, you make the transfer, and you feel nothing, or you feel a low resentment, a sense of being bled, a quiet keeping of accounts that turns every gift into a transaction. The giving has become a duty you perform and a number you track, and somewhere the joy has drained out of it, and you suspect that a gift given through clenched teeth is not really the thing the Bible was talking about.

Or maybe the church has wounded you here. Someone preached giving only when the roof leaked. Someone made you feel that your worth to the congregation was your contribution. Someone built a kingdom on guilt and gold and called it stewardship, and now the very word giving makes you flinch, because you have seen it used as a lever and a shame and a hustle. If that is you, I am sorry, and I want to say plainly that what was done to you was a distortion of something good.

Under all of it is a single buried fact, the same one for the fearful and the cold and the wounded alike. We hold money with a closed fist because we believe, somewhere below conscious thought, that it is what keeps us safe, and the open hand feels like surrender. It is surrender. That is the whole point. And the surprising news of Scripture is that the open hand is not how you lose your life. It is how you finally get free of the thing that was quietly running it.

parts.title: Why the Open Hand Matters
parts.body:
It matters because greed is the most undetectable sin you carry, and generosity is its only reliable cure. Almost no one believes they are greedy. The greedy man always points to someone richer and concludes that greed lives there, in the larger barn, never in his own. Pride knows its name, lust knows its name, anger knows its name, but greed wears the mask of prudence and responsibility and good planning, and it can run a whole life from behind that mask without ever being caught. The only thing that flushes it into the open is the act of giving, because the hand that cannot open has just told you the truth that the heart was hiding.

It matters because Jesus tied the location of your treasure to the location of your heart, and he ran the line in the direction we never expect. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Not your heart determines your treasure, but your treasure pulls your heart. Which means generosity is not merely the result of a loving heart. It is one of the ways a loving heart is made. Every gift you send ahead drags a little of your heart after it, and a person who gives steadily toward the kingdom finds, over years, that their affections have quietly relocated to where their money has been going. You can give your way into caring. You cannot merely care your way into giving.

It matters because the closed fist does not only fail to bless others. It slowly deforms the one who keeps it closed. Hoarding is not a neutral financial strategy. It is a posture of the soul, a grip that tightens over time, an anxiety that grows in proportion to the pile it is guarding, until a person discovers that they do not own their possessions, their possessions own them. The rich fool in the parable was not condemned for being wealthy. He was condemned for a soul that had shrunk to the size of his barns. Generosity is the practice that keeps the soul from shrinking.

And it matters for the watching world, which has always read the church's pocketbook more clearly than its doctrine. The pagans of the second century could argue with Christian theology, but they could not explain the Christian open hand, the way these strange people fed the poor who were not their own and buried the dead who were nobody's responsibility and gave past the point of sense. The generosity was the apologetic. It still is. A church that gives recklessly preaches a sermon no skeptic can refute, and a church that grips its gold tightly preaches a louder one in the other direction. The skeptic at the edge of the room is not weighing your statement of faith. He is weighing your statement of accounts.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Teaches About Giving
parts.body:
Start with the truth that grounds everything else, the truth the closed fist forgets. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell in it. You did not make the rain that grew the grain that built the wealth. You did not give yourself the body, the mind, the breath, the opportunity, or the country of your birth. Every dollar you have ever held passed through your hands from a hand that owns it more deeply than you ever could. The giver is never giving away what is finally his. He is releasing what was always on loan. This is why Scripture can ask for so much. It is not asking you to part with your own. It is asking you to loosen your grip on God's.

Then the tithe, which the modern church both overuses and misunderstands. Long before the law, Abraham gives a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek, and Jacob vows a tenth at Bethel, so the practice of returning a tithe to God is older than Moses. The law then builds it in, the tenth belonging to the Lord, and the prophet Malachi delivers the one place in Scripture where God invites his people to test him. Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, and see if I will not open the windows of heaven. But the tithe was never a ceiling. It was a floor, a training number, a place to begin learning the open hand, and the New Testament moves the conversation past it entirely. Jesus watches a widow drop two small coins into the treasury and says she gave more than all the rich, because they gave out of abundance and she gave out of her poverty, everything she had. He does not measure the gift by its size but by its cost. The tithe is where you start. Sacrifice is where you are headed.

Then Jesus on treasure, in the plainest financial advice he ever gave. Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. He is not against investing. He is against investing in the wrong account. Every earthly treasure is built on a foundation of decay, the moth eating the garment, the rust eating the metal, the thief taking the rest, and finally death taking it all, because there are no luggage racks on a hearse. But the treasure moved into the kingdom by an open hand is moved beyond the reach of every force that destroys. Generosity, in Jesus' accounting, is not the loss of wealth. It is the transfer of wealth into the one account that survives your funeral.

Then Paul, who gives the most psychologically precise teaching on giving in the Bible, writing to the Corinthians about a relief fund for the poor in Jerusalem. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. The word translated cheerful is the word from which we get hilarious. God is not after grim, dutiful, resentful giving. He is after the laughing kind, the kind that gives because giving has become a delight. And Paul roots it not in pressure but in the gospel itself. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. The open hand of the Christian is a response to the open hand of God, who held nothing back, who gave his own Son, who emptied himself for people who could never repay. We give because we have been given to, lavishly, while we were still closed fists ourselves.

And then the promise that the fearful giver most needs to hear, because it answers the very anxiety that keeps the hand shut. God is able to make all grace abound to you, Paul writes, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work. He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed. Notice the logic. The God who asks you to give is the God who supplies the seed in the first place and promises to keep supplying it. The open hand is not a hand that empties and stays empty. It is a hand positioned to keep receiving, because a closed fist can neither give nor be filled. You cannot pour water into a clenched hand.

parts.title: The Church of the Open Hand
parts.body:
The early church was famous in the pagan world for two things its neighbors could not understand, and both were forms of giving. The first Christians sold their possessions and shared with anyone in need, and the book of Acts records that there was not a needy person among them, a sentence that should stop us, because it describes a community that had simply solved poverty among its own by the radical practice of the open hand. They were not communists and they were not coerced, the giving was voluntary and joyful, but they held their possessions so loosely that need had nowhere to take root.

This reputation only grew. By the second century, a pagan observer named Lucian mocked the Christians for being so easily parted from their money by anyone in distress, and the contempt was itself a testimony. When a terrible plague swept the empire in the third century, the pagans fled their own dying, but the Christians stayed to nurse the sick, often catching the disease and dying themselves, and the bishop Dionysius wrote that they did it gladly, drawing the sickness of their neighbors onto themselves. A century later the emperor Julian, who hated the faith and tried to revive paganism, complained bitterly in a letter that the impious Galileans support not only their own poor but ours as well, and that the lack of such charity among his own priests was losing him the empire. The church conquered Rome, in part, with casseroles and bedpans and an open hand the world had never seen.

The fathers preached this with a bluntness that would empty a modern sanctuary. Basil of Caesarea, in the fourth century, built an entire complex for the poor and the sick on the edge of his city, a place so large it was called a new town, and he told the rich to their faces that the bread you hold is the bread of the hungry, the coat in your closet belongs to the naked, the shoes rotting in your house belong to the barefoot. John Chrysostom, preaching amid the wealth of Constantinople, said flatly that not to share our own wealth with the poor is robbery, that the rich are merely the stewards of what belongs to the destitute. Ambrose of Milan said you are not making a gift of your possessions to the poor, you are handing them back what is theirs. These were not radicals at the edge. They were the central pastors of the church, working out what the open hand actually costs.

The monastic movement carried the witness in a different key, through voluntary poverty, and Francis of Assisi remains its most beautiful and unsettling example. The son of a wealthy cloth merchant, he stripped off his fine clothing in the public square of Assisi in the year 1206, handed it back to his furious father, and walked away with nothing, and somehow walked away singing. Few are called to that literal stripping. But the tradition kept the witness alive on purpose, as a standing rebuke to the assumption that more is always better and security always lies in the pile, because here was a man with nothing who was demonstrably the most joyful person anyone had met.

The Reformers brought a needed correction, recovering the dignity of ordinary earning and saving, but the best of them kept the open hand central. John Wesley, in the eighteenth century, preached a sermon on the use of money with three plain points, earn all you can, save all you can, give all you can, and he warned that most people stop after the first two and lock the door against the third. He lived it with a severity that shames us. As his book royalties multiplied and his income grew thirtyfold over his life, he held his own spending flat, deciding what he needed and giving away everything above that line, so that he died having given away a fortune and leaving almost nothing behind. The line, Wesley saw, must be drawn on the keeping, not the earning. Earn freely, even abundantly. But cap the keeping, and let the open hand carry the rest.

And the tradition has always had to name a counterfeit, because the open hand has a dark imitation that preys on the poor in Jesus' name. The prosperity gospel, a creature of the twentieth century, teaches that giving is a financial technique, that you give in order to get, that the seed you sow into the ministry will return to you multiplied in cash. It takes the joy of the open hand and turns it into the greed of the closed one, giving as an investment scheme, generosity as a down payment on getting rich. It is a lie, and it is cruel, because it most often empties the pockets of the desperate to fill the pockets of the preacher. No one reading this page should hear any echo of it here. The open hand gives expecting nothing back in this life, because it has already received everything in Christ.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Christians have nothing to fear from honest research on giving, because all truth is God's truth, and the labs have spent the last several decades confirming what the Bible assumed, that the open hand is good for the one who opens it. We can read this work with gratitude and without surprise, and then test it, because measuring that generosity makes people happier is not the same as knowing what generosity is finally for. What follows takes five bodies of secular knowledge seriously and tests each against Scripture.

secular.source: The research on generosity and happiness
secular.author: Elizabeth Dunn and Michael Norton
secular.whatItGetsRight: In a now-famous set of experiments published as Happy Money, Dunn and Norton showed that people made measurably happier by spending money on others than on themselves, that the boost from giving is real, replicable, and visible even in small children and across cultures, and that prosocial spending lifts well-being in a way that buying for oneself reliably fails to do. The closed fist, the data says, is bad for the person who keeps it closed.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research confirms what Jesus said, that it is more blessed to give than to receive, and it is striking to watch a laboratory stumble onto a sentence from Acts. But the science can only measure the warm feeling and recommend giving as a path to personal happiness, which quietly turns the gift into one more thing the self consumes for its own benefit. Scripture cuts deeper. The point of the open hand is not that giving feels good. It is that giving frees you from the false god of Mammon and conforms you to the self-emptying God who gave his Son. The happiness is a byproduct, never the aim. Give in order to feel good, and you have not escaped the self. You have just found a more pleasant way to serve it.

secular.author: Robert Lupton
secular.whatItGetsRight: Lupton sounds a hard and needed warning that giving can wound the very people it means to help, that one-way charity which does for people what they could do for themselves can erode dignity, create dependency, and leave the giver feeling generous while the recipient is quietly diminished. He insists that real generosity respects the agency and the gifts of the poor, builds reciprocity rather than charity, and asks the harder question of what actually helps rather than what merely feels charitable.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture would receive this correction gladly, because it never romanticized handouts. The law commanded gleaning, which left the harvest in the field for the poor to gather with their own hands, dignity and provision together, and Paul insisted that those who could work should work. But Lupton's frame, left alone, can harden into an excuse for the closed fist, a sophisticated reason to give less, since one can always claim a gift might create dependency. Scripture keeps both truths. Give wisely, in ways that honor the dignity of the poor, and give generously, even recklessly, because the Samaritan did not run a needs assessment on the man in the ditch. He bound the wounds and paid the bill. Wisdom in giving must never become a permission slip for withholding.

secular.author: Daniel Kahneman, Richard Thaler and the field of nudge research
secular.whatItGetsRight: Behavioral economists have shown that giving is powerfully shaped by how the choice is framed, that automatic and default arrangements dramatically increase generosity, that we give more when the need has a face rather than a statistic, and that the painless structure of giving before the money ever feels like ours, through automatic transfer, defeats the procrastination and the loss aversion that otherwise shrink every gift. The wiring that makes us hold on can be worked with rather than merely fought.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: This is genuinely useful, and Scripture would not despise it. Paul's own counsel to set aside a sum on the first day of every week, before life crowds it out, is a kind of ancient default setting, generosity made automatic so that it does not have to win a fresh battle against fear each month. But the nudge can only rearrange the behavior. It cannot change the heart that needs nudging, and a person can be nudged into giving while remaining, underneath, a worshiper of Mammon who simply gives on autopilot. Scripture wants the structure and the transformed wanter both. Automate the gift, yes, to defeat the resistance. But do not mistake an automated transfer for a converted heart. God is after a cheerful giver, not merely a well-defaulted one.

secular.source: The studies on wealth and compassion
secular.author: Paul Piff and the social psychology of class
secular.whatItGetsRight: Piff and his colleagues produced a striking body of research suggesting that, in many measured situations, increasing wealth correlates with decreasing generosity and empathy, that the rich often give a smaller percentage than the poor, and that the experience of abundance can subtly reduce attentiveness to the needs of others. The data quietly confirms an uncomfortable pattern, that the more we have, the harder the hand becomes to open.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture saw this with terrible clarity. It is the rich young ruler who walks away sorrowful, the rich fool who builds bigger barns, the camel and the needle's eye, the warning that those who desire to be rich fall into a snare. Jesus did not hate the rich, he loved the young ruler as he watched him leave, but he understood that wealth has a gravitational pull on the soul that grows stronger with the pile. The research measures the symptom. Scripture names the disease and offers the only cure, which is not less wealth necessarily but the deliberate, joyful, repeated practice of the open hand, the giving that breaks the grip before the grip can close for good. Piff can show you the danger. Only grace and practice can get you free of it.

secular.source: Effective altruism and the ethics of giving
secular.author: Peter Singer and the effective altruism movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: Singer presses an uncomfortable and clarifying question, that if we would ruin our shoes to save a drowning child in front of us, we cannot easily justify spending on luxuries while children die of preventable causes we could address from a distance. The effective altruism movement insists that giving be taken seriously as a moral obligation, directed toward where it does the most measurable good, and that comfortable people examine honestly how much they could give and do not.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The challenge is bracing, and Scripture would amplify rather than soften the demand, for the Bible asks more of the rich than Singer does, not less. But effective altruism rests the obligation on a cold utilitarian calculus, a math of maximized welfare that has no place for the giver's heart, the recipient's face, or the God to whom both belong. It can tell you to give and even where, but it gives you no joy in the giving and no gospel underneath it, only a relentless moral arithmetic that crushes more than it frees. Scripture grounds generosity not in obligation but in grace received, in the God who gave first and lavishly, so that the open hand becomes worship rather than tax. Singer can make you feel you ought to give. The gospel can make you want to.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and the same call to generosity still order their giving along two different lines, and the difference is not careless. It runs to the question of structure, whether the open hand is best trained by a fixed and steady discipline or best expressed by a free and Spirit-led responsiveness to need. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are guarding something real, and both have a danger they are watching against.

views.view: The disciplined tithe as the trellis for generosity
views.body: This view holds that generosity, like every other virtue, needs structure to survive, and that the historic practice of the tithe, a fixed proportion returned to God first, off the top, before any other claim, is the trellis on which a life of giving grows. Feelings are fickle and need is endless, and a generosity that waits to be moved will, in most months, simply not be moved, crowded out by the thousand pressing claims of ordinary life. Advocates of this view point to the deep biblical roots of proportional giving, from Abraham's tenth to Jacob's vow to the law's command to Malachi's invitation to test God, and they argue that a percentage decided in advance and given without renegotiation each month is how an ordinary believer actually escapes the gravity of greed. They will tell you that the discipline is freedom, that giving first turns the rest of the budget into the leftovers rather than the priority, and that the tithe is meant to be a floor you build on, not a cap you stop at. But hear the steelman clearly. This view insists the tithe must never become a transaction that buys off God or a ceiling that lets the wealthy give a painless tenth and grip the rest, and the careful advocate keeps pressing past the floor toward sacrifice, lest the discipline calcify into a tidy religious tax that leaves the heart unchanged.

views.view: Spirit-led generosity beyond all fixed measures
views.body: This view holds that the New Testament deliberately moves past the tithe into a freedom that no fixed percentage can contain, and that the open hand is meant to respond to the actual need in front of it and the actual prompting of the Spirit, not to a number set once and never revisited. Jesus praised a widow who gave everything and a Samaritan who gave whatever the wounded man required, and the early church sold possessions as needs arose rather than calculating a tenth. Advocates of this view worry that a fixed tithe can become a comfortable stopping point, a way for the prosperous to feel generous while withholding the abundance God actually entrusted to them, and they call instead for a giving that is sacrificial, responsive, and unbounded, that asks not what percentage satisfies the rule but what love requires in this case, for this person, in this season. They will tell you that the Spirit-led giver, holding everything loosely, often gives far past a tenth, and finds joy precisely in the freedom from the ledger. But hear the steelman clearly. This view insists that freedom from a fixed measure must never become freedom from any measure at all, the kind of vague generosity that intends much and gives little, and the careful advocate builds real, sacrificial, accountable giving into actual practice, lest holy freedom dissolve into a sentiment that never reaches the hand.

parts.title: What Generosity Forms in a Person
parts.body:
You will not think your way to an open hand. I have read the verses about giving for thirty years, and they have never once, by themselves, loosened my grip in the moment the gift was actually leaving. The heart is not persuaded by information. It is retrained by practice, the way a hand is opened not by understanding openness but by opening, again and again, until the opening becomes who you are. And along the way God forms specific things in the one who keeps practicing the open hand, things the closed fist never produces.

He forms freedom from Mammon, which is the first and deepest work. Money makes a quiet claim on every soul, the claim to be the thing that keeps you safe, and as long as that claim goes unchallenged it grows, until a person serves the very wealth they think they own. Every act of giving is a small defection from that kingdom, a public declaration to your own heart that money is not your god, that you can let it go and survive, that your security rests somewhere the market cannot reach. Give long enough and the grip you could not pray away simply loosens, not because you tried harder but because you practiced surrender until surrender became habit.

He forms trust, because the open hand is, at bottom, a wager on the character of God. The fearful fist says it is all up to me, the future is mine to secure, the wall between my family and ruin is built of dollars I dare not release. The open hand says something else. It says the God who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies and gave his own Son will not abandon me, that I can give because I am held, that the seed released to others is released into the keeping of the One who supplies all seed. You cannot give generously and anxiously for long. Eventually one of them has to go, and grace sees to it that the giving outlasts the fear.

He forms compassion, the relocated heart, because where your treasure goes your affections follow. The believer who begins giving to the poor, even mechanically, even coldly, finds over years that the poor have somehow become real to them, that a category has become a face, that they have started to care about what they fund. This is the law Jesus named running in reverse from how we expect. We assume we will give to what we love. He tells us we will come to love what we give to, and it is true, and it is one of the kindest mechanisms God ever built into a soul.

And he forms joy, the hilarious cheerfulness Paul named, which is the strangest fruit of all, because the closed fist always believes that joy lies in keeping and giving is the loss of it. Then a person actually gives, sacrificially, freely, and discovers the thing the rich fool never learned and the widow knew by heart, that the open hand is the lighter one, that the grip was the burden all along, and that a life poured out in the direction of others is not the life you lose but the life you finally get to keep. He who loses his life will find it. The open hand is that sentence, made daily, in the currency of an ordinary checkbook.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: None of this earns you anything from God, and none of it is a technique for getting rich, and if your situation involves real hardship, the bills you cannot cover, the choice between groceries and the heating bill, then your first faithful steps are honest help and community, not heroic giving, and there is no shame in that order. The widow's two coins were counted as more than all the rest, which means God does the math differently than the donor wall does. Start where you are, this week, with one thing, and let the hand learn to open slowly, the way it learned to close.

steps: Give one gift this week that is anonymous and unrecoverable, with no receipt, no thanks, and no tax letter, simply to feel what your hand does when there is nothing to gain. Notice the resistance, and give anyway.

Look honestly at where your money actually went last month and ask what it says you love, because your spending is a more candid confession than your prayers. Write one sentence naming what you found.

Pick one specific person or need with a face, not a category, and meet it this week, learning generosity first in the particular before you ever systematize it. The Samaritan helped a man, not a cause.
Pray over the closed fist itself, naming the fear underneath it out loud to God, the dread of not having enough, and ask him to begin loosening what you cannot loosen by willpower.

Make your giving the first line of your budget rather than the last, deciding the amount in advance and moving it before the rest of life can spend it. Generosity that waits for leftovers waits forever.

Set a proportion and automate it, defeating the monthly battle against fear by giving before the money ever feels like yours, the way Paul told the Corinthians to set aside a sum on the first day of every week.

Tell one trusted person what you actually give, breaking the secrecy that lets generosity stay vague, and invite them to ask you about it, because a discipline no one can see is a discipline that quietly erodes.

Examine one place where you have used wisdom as a cover for the closed fist, a gift you talked yourself out of by worrying it might create dependency, and ask whether that was discernment or fear wearing its mask.

Push past the floor toward something that costs you, raising your giving to a level you can actually feel, because the widow was praised not for the size of her gift but for the size of what it cost her.

Do a possessions audit this season with Basil's sentence in your ears, that the coat in your closet belongs to the naked, and let one genuinely useful thing you have been hoarding reach the person who needs it.

Build generosity into your household on purpose so your children see the open hand, letting them watch you give, letting them give from their own small money, and telling them why, because they are learning a god from you either way.

Pick one ongoing need to commit to for the long haul rather than only responding to crises, letting your heart relocate over time toward the people and the work you steadily fund, so that giving forms affection and not only relief.

Draw your line on the keeping, not the earning, the way Wesley did, deciding what is enough for your household, writing it down with a spouse or wise friend, and letting everything above that line carry someone else's name before it arrives.

Let your giving rise as your income rises rather than letting your lifestyle absorb every gain, so that abundance becomes more open hand rather than a thicker cushion, and the danger Piff measured never gets its grip on you.

Plan your generosity past your own death, deciding now what your estate will do for the kingdom and the poor, treating even what you leave behind as treasure to be sent ahead rather than a final hoard to be passed down.

Make the open hand the settled posture of a lifetime, not a season's experiment, until giving has stopped being a decision you agonize over and become simply the way you hold everything, loosely, gratefully, as a steward of what was always God's, with your heart already where your treasure has gone.
